title: The ones who carry it
hook: millions have memorized the whole Qur'an, many as children

segments.voice: Yesterday, qira'at: the readings, passed down in chains of reciters. Your line was many voices, one text.

In a small room in Cairo, or Kano, or Karachi, or a converted storefront in Minneapolis, a boy of eleven stands before his teacher and a row of family. He recites. Not a surah: the whole Qur'an, from al-Fatiha to An-Nas, from memory, for hours, while the teacher follows along and listens for a single slip. When he finishes, his mother is crying. There's a word for what he has become.
screen: `A BOY OF ELEVEN STANDS UP.` → `THE WHOLE QUR'AN, FROM MEMORY.` → `HIS MOTHER IS CRYING.`

segments.voice: The word is hafiz; for a woman, hafizah. It comes from a root meaning to guard, to preserve, to keep, and that root is in the Qur'an itself. In Pickthall's words: "Lo! We, even We, reveal the Reminder, and lo! We verily are its Guardian." Guardian there comes from the same root. In the tradition, the memorizers are part of how that guarding happens: the book is kept not only on paper but in people. Nobody keeps a count of them. Often they begin as children, in schools built for exactly this, a few lines at a time, reciting each day's new portion to a teacher and revising the old. The Qur'an seems made for it; its rhythm and rhyme hold together in the memory. It says of itself, in Pickthall: "And in truth We have made the Qur'an easy to remember; but is there any that remembereth?" The Prophet ﷺ spoke about those who carry it. A hadith says the one who recites skillfully will be with the noble, righteous scribes, the angels; and the one who recites with difficulty, stumbling over it, gets a double reward. Stumbling, and still going, counts twice. The title even reached poetry: tradition says the Persian poet Hafez of Shiraz took his name because he knew the Qur'an by heart. And it isn't finished when the last surah is learned. Keeping it is its own work. The Prophet compared it to a hobbled camel: tend it, or it slips away.
screen: `HAFIZ: ONE WHO GUARDS AND KEEPS` · `KEPT IN PEOPLE, OFTEN FROM CHILDHOOD` · `STUMBLING COUNTS TWICE` · `TEND IT, LIKE A HOBBLED CAMEL`

segments.voice: Choose one short verse you don't know yet: the second line of al-Ikhlas, Allahus-samad, is a gentle start, or any short line you'd like to keep. Say it five times slowly while looking at it, then five times with your eyes closed, and if you stumble, it counts. If you're here to learn about the path rather than to practice it, learn the verse's meaning by heart instead.
Hafiz. One who has memorized the whole Qur'an: literally a guardian, a keeper. For a woman, hafizah. Today's word.
Your line: carried by heart. One verse, kept and tended, is a real beginning. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Muslim children and adults memorize the Qur'an in dedicated schools and circles, reciting a new portion to a teacher each day and revising what they know; a hafiz often leads the long Ramadan night prayers.
